newsitem.title: UK: Key points of the British budget.
newsitem.headline: Key points of the British budget.

text.p: Following is a summary of key points from Britain's budget, the first one by a Labour government since 1978, as presented by Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown on Wednesday.
-- Fiscal policy will be tightened by a net 5.5 billion stg this year and by 4.75 billion next year.
-- A "windfall tax" on utilities will raise a net 4.8 billion stg. Brown detailed 2.1 bln stg from electricity, 1.65 billion from water and 1.45 from others.
-- GDP was estimated to grow by 3.25 percent this year and 2.5 percent next year.
-- Inflation was estimated at 2.5 percent in 1997, 2.75 percent in 1998 and 2.5 percent in 1999.
-- The public sector borrowing requirement (PSBR) was estimated at 13.25 billion stg in 1997 and 5.5 billion in 1998.
-- Consumer spending growth was estimated at 4.5 percent for 1997 and 4.0 percent for 1998.
-- Tax credits on Advance Corporation Tax paid to pension funds would be abolished.
-- Brown said he shared industry concerns over the strength of sterling and would take steps to address them.
-- Mortgage interest relief (MIRAS) was cut to 10 percent from 15 percent starting in April 1998.
-- Stamp duty was raised to 1.5 percent on transactions of more than 250,000 stg and 2.0 percent on those over 500,000 stg.
-- Main corporate tax rates were cut by 2.0 percentage points to 31 percent starting April 1997 (rpt 1997), and the tax rate on small companies was cut to 21 percent from 23 percent.
-- No changes were made to income tax rates, but Brown said a 10-pence starting rate of income tax would be introduced as soon as it was prudent to do so.
-- VAT on domestic fuel and power consumption was cut to 5.0 percent from 8.0 percent effective Sept 1, while there would be no extenstion of VAT to food, children's clothes and newspapers.
-- Duty on petrol and diesel was increased with immediate effect, with the price of petrol rising by four pence a litre.
-- Alcohol duties would be raised by inflation only pending a cross-border review. Tobacco tax was raised by another two percent.
-- Excise duties on lorries and buses that meet low emission standards were cut.
-- Private medical insurance tax relief abolished for over-60s.
-- The government will allocate 3.5 billion stg to "welfare-to-work" programmes to get young unemployed people off welfare and back into jobs or training.
-- Government spending on health was estimated to rise by 5.0 percent, or 2.25 percent in real terms. Education will be allocated 1.3 billion stg over the course of the current parliament.
-- London Newsroom, +44-171-542-6721
